title: Corruption Cases in the DEA Show the US Must Address Its Responsibilities in the Fight Against the ‘Narco,’ Sheinbaum Says
author: Arturo Sánchez Jiménez and Alma E. Muñoz
content:
_This article by Arturo Sánchez Jiménez and Alma E. Muñoz originally appeared
in the[September 8, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/09/08/politica/casos-de-
corrupcion-en-la-dea-muestran-que-eu-debe-atender-sus-responsabilidades-en-
combate-al-narco-sheinbaum), Mexico's premier left wing daily newspaper._

**Mexico City**. Recent corruption cases among agents of the United States
Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) show that that country must also address
its own responsibilities in the fight against drug trafficking, President
Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo said this Tuesday at her usual press conference at the
National Palace. She was responding to a question about whether the United
States is doing "its part" on security cooperation.

> We insist that they have a very important part to carry out over there, and
> not just keep mentioning Mexico.
>
> President Claudia Sheinbaum

In that context, the president referred to a recent case in which DEA agents
were arrested for corruption, insisting that Washington has pending matters to
resolve on its own territory. She recalled that**fentanyl trafficking from
Mexico "has been reduced by more than 70 percent, acknowledged by them,"** and
stressed that methamphetamine is also produced in the United States, "so much
so that there was a television series dedicated to it," in addition to
distribution and money laundering taking place there, "because**there is more
consumption over there.** "

The head of the Executive highlighted that the director of the Office of
National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), Sara Carter, has acknowledged the need
to address drug consumption as a public health problem. On Carter, she
recalled that the official "recently released a document… very interesting,
because **in that document, for the first time, they recognize the need to
address drug consumption as a national public health policy. "**

She added that Carter visited Mexico, took an interest in the actions being
undertaken in the country to address the causes of violence and prevent drug
consumption, such as the Boxing for Peace program, and had planned to return
soon, since she was also interested in the Mexico Sings (México Canta) program
in the United States. "I don't know how much progress they've made, but at
least there is now an acknowledgment," she stated, comparing that stance with
the anti-drug campaign led by Nancy Reagan in the 1980s: "Now it is Sara
Carter who acknowledges."
